title: Your one-page profit plan, price changes and monthly review

say: Your one-page profit plan, price changes, and a monthly review.
This is the video for Module 4 of Pricing, Costing and Profit Planning.
In this final module, everything comes together on one page, with every number agreeing with the others. First, your cost table and unit cost.
Second, your price and contribution per unit.
Third, your break-even point.
Fourth, your profit target, turned into weekly sales.
And fifth, a projected profit and loss, with notes on how you will manage cash. Use your own real numbers, and label any estimate honestly.
Here is a service business. Halima's fixed costs, including her own wage of 70,000 naira, are 155,000 naira a month.
Each gown uses 4,400 naira of materials, so her contribution is 10,600 naira.
155,000 divided by 10,600 is 14.6. So she breaks even at 15 gowns, and needs 23 gowns to hit her 80,000 naira target. She plans 25, at 375,000 naira of sales.
Take away 110,000 naira of materials and 155,000 naira of fixed costs.
Her projected net profit is 110,000 naira, well within her capacity.
She takes a 50 percent deposit of 7,500 naira, which covers the materials, so she never funds them from her own pocket.
Check your plan. Every fixed cost appears once, including your wage. The same variable cost is used everywhere. Break-even and target are rounded up, and both are below what you can really produce.
Your cash notes say how you will fund materials, and every price is dated.

panel.heading: Checks for your plan
items: Your wage and equipment wear included

say: A discount comes straight out of your contribution.
Ngozi earns 760 naira contribution per pack, 152,000 naira a month.
At 10 percent off, the price is 1,530 naira and contribution falls to 590 naira. She would need 258 packs, 29 percent more sales, just to stand still.
So she offers a bundle instead: 5 packs for 8,000 naira, which still earns 660 naira a pack.
When flour rises from 15,000 to 18,000 naira, Ngozi recalculates. That is 60 naira more per pack, so her variable cost becomes 1,000 naira.

say: Use one formula: profit equals units sold times contribution per unit, minus fixed costs. Change one number at a time.
Ngozi's base profit is 250 times 760, minus 110,000. That is 80,000 naira.
A 100 naira price rise lifts profit to 105,000 naira.
A 10 percent rise in variable cost drops it to 56,500 naira. And a 20 percent fall in sales drops it to 42,000 naira.
So protecting price and volume matters most, and cost rises must be passed on quickly.

To remember. Keep your plan on one page, with every number agreeing. Keep targets within your capacity. Add value instead of cutting price. When costs rise, recalculate first, then give notice. And review your numbers every month.

panel.heading: Remember
items: One page, and every number agrees
Break-even and target below your capacity
Bundles protect your price better than cuts
When costs rise, recalculate, then give notice
Review P&L, prices, cash and targets monthly
